title: Forms of attack
starter: Choose a cyberattack that has been in the news. Write down who was attacked, what the attackers wanted, and what it cost the organisation.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What is a cyberattack?
facts: An attempt to damage or disrupt a system, or to gain unauthorised access to it or its data.
Attacks can come from outside the network or from inside it.
The people who carry them out are often called hackers or attackers.
stations.challenge: Write your own definition of a cyberattack.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: An attempt to damage or disrupt a system, or to gain unauthorised access to it or its data.
Also credit: Attacks can come from outside the network or from inside it.

questions.a: An attempt to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a system or its data
Both outside the network and inside it

stations.name: The six forms of attack
facts: Malware, social engineering (including phishing), brute-force attacks, denial of service, data interception and theft, and SQL injection.
Some attack the technology; others attack the people using it.
stations.challenge: Which of the six forms of attack targets people rather than computers?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Malware, social engineering (including phishing), brute-force attacks, denial of service, data interception and theft, and SQL injection.
Also credit: Some attack the technology; others attack the people using it.

questions.q: Match each form of attack to what it does.
questions.a: Malware → Malicious software that damages or takes control of a system; Phishing → Fake messages that trick people into giving away information; Brute-force attack → Trying huge numbers of passwords until one works; Denial of service → Flooding a server with requests so it can't respond; Data interception → Capturing data as it travels across a network; SQL injection → Entering code into a text box to attack a database

stations.name: What do attackers want?
facts: Money: ransoms, fraud and selling stolen data.
Data: personal details, passwords, company secrets.
Disruption: damaging a rival, making a political point, or simply showing off.
stations.challenge: Suggest two reasons someone might attack a school's network.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Money: ransoms, fraud and selling stolen data.
Also credit: Data: personal details, passwords, company secrets.

questions.q: Why do most criminal cyberattacks happen?
A pen tester is paid by a company to attack its systems. Is this a crime?
questions.a: No, because the company has given permission

stations.name: CryptoLocker
facts: CryptoLocker was ransomware that appeared in 2013 and encrypted victims' files.
Victims were told to pay a ransom in Bitcoin to get their files back.
It spread through infected email attachments and a botnet.
stations.challenge: Answer the starter questions about CryptoLocker.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: CryptoLocker was ransomware that appeared in 2013 and encrypted victims' files.
Also credit: Victims were told to pay a ransom in Bitcoin to get their files back.

questions.q: What type of malware was CryptoLocker?
How did most victims get infected?
questions.a: By opening an infected email attachment

stations.name: Operation Tovar
facts: In 2014, police forces and security companies from several countries worked together to take down the botnet behind CryptoLocker.
The operation was called Operation Tovar.
The FBI offered a reward of up to $3 million for information leading to the arrest of Evgeniy Bogachev, who has never been caught.
stations.challenge: Why do cybercrime investigations need international cooperation?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: In 2014, police forces and security companies from several countries worked together to take down the botnet behind CryptoLocker.
Also credit: The operation was called Operation Tovar.

questions.a: An international operation that took down the botnet behind CryptoLocker
Attackers can operate from another country, hiding their identity and location

stations.name: How much damage?
facts: CryptoLocker is estimated to have extorted around $3 million from victims before it was shut down.
The cost of an attack isn't only the ransom: there's downtime, lost data, recovery and damage to reputation.
Organisations can also be fined if they fail to protect personal data.
stations.challenge: List four costs to a school if its network were attacked.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: CryptoLocker is estimated to have extorted around $3 million from victims before it was shut down.
Also credit: The cost of an attack isn't only the ransom: there's downtime, lost data, recovery and damage to reputation.

questions.q: Which of these are costs of a successful attack on a business? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Downtime while systems are offline; Money spent recovering data; Damage to the company's reputation; Possible fines for failing to protect personal data

final.name: Final challenge: name that attack

questions.q: Which form of attack does each incident describe?
questions.a: An email pretending to be from the bank asks for a password = Phishing; Software downloaded with a game secretly deletes files = Malware; A program tries a million passwords on one account = Brute force; A website is flooded with fake requests until it goes offline = Denial of service; A text message claims a parcel is waiting and links to a fake login page = Phishing; A program encrypts files and demands a payment = Malware; Thousands of infected computers send traffic to one server at once = Denial of service; A dictionary of common passwords is tried against a login page = Brute force

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Name two forms of attack that target people rather than software.
points: Some attack the technology; others attack the people using it.
The people who carry them out are often called hackers or attackers.
The cost of an attack isn't only the ransom: there's downtime, lost data, recovery and damage to reputation.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
